paragraphs: Dmitri Fyodorovitch was a young man of twenty-eight, of medium height and pleasant appearance, but he looked older than his years. He was muscular and plainly very strong. Yet there was something unhealthy in his face. It was rather thin, his cheeks were hollow, and their color was an unwholesome yellow. His large, dark, prominent eyes looked firmly determined, and yet there was something vague in them too. Even when he was excited and talking angrily, his eyes somehow did not follow his mood. They showed something else, sometimes quite out of keeping with what was going on. “It’s hard to tell what he’s thinking,” people who talked to him would sometimes say. Those who saw something brooding and sullen in his eyes were startled by his sudden laugh, which showed that cheerful, light-hearted thoughts were in his head at the very moment when his eyes were so gloomy. It was easy to understand the strained look on his face just now. Everyone knew, or had heard, how wild and dissolute a life he had been leading lately, and how violent his rage had been in his quarrels with his father. Several stories about it were going around town. It is true that he was hot-tempered by nature, “of an unstable and unbalanced mind,” as our justice of the peace, Katchalnikov, aptly described him.

He was dressed stylishly and faultlessly, in a frock-coat buttoned with care. He wore black gloves and carried a top hat. Since he had left the army only recently, he still had a mustache and no beard. His dark brown hair was cropped short and combed forward over his temples. He walked with the long, determined stride of a soldier. He stood still for a moment on the threshold, glanced over the whole party, and went straight up to the elder, guessing that he was their host. He made him a deep bow and asked for his blessing. Father Zossima rose in his chair and blessed him. Dmitri respectfully kissed his hand and said, with intense feeling, almost with anger:

“Please be so kind as to forgive me for keeping you waiting so long. But Smerdyakov, the servant my father sent me, told me twice over, when I asked him, that the appointment was for one o’clock. Now I suddenly learn—”
“Don’t trouble yourself,” the elder broke in. “It doesn’t matter. You are a little late. It’s of no consequence....”
“I’m extremely grateful to you, and I expected no less of your kindness.”

With these words Dmitri bowed once more. Then he turned suddenly to his father and made him a bow just as low and respectful. He had clearly thought it out beforehand, and he made this bow in all seriousness, believing it his duty to show his respect and good intentions.

Fyodor Pavlovitch was caught off guard, but he rose to the occasion. In answer to Dmitri’s bow he jumped up from his chair and bowed to his son just as low. His face was suddenly solemn and impressive, which gave him a downright spiteful look. Dmitri bowed to the whole company, and without a word walked over to the window with his long, resolute stride. He sat down on the only empty chair, near Father Païssy, and leaning forward, got ready to listen to the conversation he had interrupted.

Dmitri’s entrance had taken no more than two minutes, and the conversation started up again. But this time Miüsov did not think it necessary to answer Father Païssy’s insistent and almost irritable question.

“Allow me to withdraw from this discussion,” he said, with a certain well-bred offhandedness. “It’s a subtle question, too. Look, Ivan Fyodorovitch is smiling at us. He must have something interesting to say about it as well. Ask him.”

“Nothing special, just one small remark,” Ivan answered at once. “European Liberals in general, and even our own liberal dabblers, often confuse the final results of socialism with those of Christianity. This wild notion is, of course, characteristic of them. But it’s not only Liberals and dabblers who confuse socialism with Christianity. In many cases, it seems, the police do the same—the foreign police, of course. Your Paris anecdote is rather to the point, Pyotr Alexandrovitch.”

“I ask your permission to drop this subject altogether,” Miüsov said again. “Instead, gentlemen, I’ll tell you another interesting and rather characteristic anecdote about Ivan Fyodorovitch himself. Only five days ago, at a gathering here, mostly of ladies, he declared solemnly in an argument that there was nothing in the whole world to make men love their neighbors. That there was no law of nature that man should love mankind, and that if there had been any love on earth so far, it was not because of a natural law, but simply because men have believed in immortality. Ivan Fyodorovitch added, in parenthesis, that the whole of natural law lies in that belief, and that if you were to destroy mankind’s belief in immortality, not only love but every living force that keeps the world alive would dry up at once. Moreover, nothing would then be immoral, and everything would be lawful, even cannibalism. That’s not all. He ended by claiming that for every individual like ourselves who believes in neither God nor immortality, the natural moral law must immediately turn into the exact opposite of the old religious law. Egoism, even to the point of crime, would become not only lawful but even recognized as the inevitable, the most rational, even the most honorable outcome of his position. From this paradox, gentlemen, you can judge the rest of the theories of our eccentric and paradoxical friend Ivan Fyodorovitch.”

“Excuse me,” Dmitri cried suddenly, “if I’ve heard right, then crime must not only be permitted but even recognized as the inevitable and most rational outcome of his position, for every unbeliever! Is that so or not?”
“Quite so,” said Father Païssy.
“I’ll remember that.”
Having said this, Dmitri fell silent as suddenly as he had started. Everyone looked at him with curiosity.
“Is that really your conviction about what follows when faith in immortality disappears?” the elder suddenly asked Ivan.
“Yes. That was my claim. There is no virtue if there is no immortality.”
“You are blessed if you believe that, or else you are very unhappy.”
“Why unhappy?” Ivan asked, smiling.
“Because in all probability you don’t believe in the immortality of your own soul, or in what you wrote yourself in your article on Church jurisdiction.”
“Perhaps you’re right! ... But I wasn’t altogether joking,” Ivan suddenly and strangely admitted, flushing quickly.

“You were not altogether joking. That’s true. The question is still troubling your heart, and it has not been answered. But the sufferer sometimes likes to amuse himself with his despair, as if driven to it by despair itself. Meanwhile, in your despair, you amuse yourself too, with magazine articles and talk in society, though you don’t believe your own arguments and mock them inwardly, with an aching heart.... That question you have not answered, and it is your great grief, for it demands an answer.”
“But can it be answered by me? Answered in the affirmative?” Ivan went on asking in the same strange way, still looking at the elder with the same inexplicable smile.

“If it can’t be decided in the affirmative, it will never be decided in the negative. You know that this is the peculiarity of your heart, and all its suffering comes from it. But thank the Creator, who has given you a lofty heart, capable of such suffering, of thinking and seeking higher things, for our dwelling is in the heavens. God grant that your heart finds the answer while you are on earth, and may God bless your path.”

The elder raised his hand and would have made the sign of the cross over Ivan from where he stood. But Ivan rose from his seat, went up to him, received his blessing, kissed his hand, and went back to his place in silence. His face looked firm and earnest. This act, and the whole conversation before it, which was so surprising coming from Ivan, struck everyone as strange and somehow solemn. All were silent for a moment, and there was a look almost of fear on Alyosha’s face. But Miüsov suddenly shrugged his shoulders. And at the same moment Fyodor Pavlovitch jumped up from his seat.

“Most pious and holy elder,” he cried, pointing to Ivan, “that is my son, flesh of my flesh, the dearest of my flesh! He is my most dutiful Karl Moor, so to speak, while this son who has just come in, Dmitri, against whom I am seeking justice from you, is the undutiful Franz Moor. They are both out of Schiller’s _Robbers_, and so I am the reigning Count von Moor! Judge and save us! We need not only your prayers but your prophecies!”

“Speak without clowning, and don’t begin by insulting the members of your family,” answered the elder, in a faint, exhausted voice. He was clearly getting more and more tired, and his strength was failing.

“A shameful farce, which I knew would happen when I came here!” cried Dmitri indignantly. He too leapt up. “Forgive it, reverend Father,” he added, turning to the elder. “I am not a cultivated man, and I don’t even know how to address you properly. But you have been deceived, and you were too good-natured to let us meet here. All my father wants is a scandal. Why he wants it, only he can tell. He always has some motive. But I think I know why—”

“They all blame me, all of them!” cried Fyodor Pavlovitch in his turn. “Pyotr Alexandrovitch here blames me too. You have been blaming me, Pyotr Alexandrovitch, you have!” he turned suddenly to Miüsov, though Miüsov was not dreaming of interrupting him. “They all accuse me of hiding the children’s money in my boots and cheating them. But isn’t there a court of law? There they’ll work it out for you, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, from your notes, your letters and your agreements: how much money you had, how much you’ve spent, and how much you have left. Why does Pyotr Alexandrovitch refuse to pass judgment? Dmitri is no stranger to him. Because they are all against me, while Dmitri Fyodorovitch is in debt to me, and not a little, but some thousands, of which I have documentary proof. The whole town is ringing with his debaucheries. And where he was stationed before, he several times spent a thousand or two on the seduction of some respectable girl. We know all about that, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, down to the most secret details. I’ll prove it.... Would you believe it, holy Father, he has won the heart of the most honorable of young ladies, of good family and fortune, the daughter of a gallant colonel, his former superior officer, who had received many honors and wore the Anna Order on his breast. He compromised the girl with a promise of marriage. Now she is an orphan and she is here; she is engaged to him, yet before her very eyes he is dancing attendance on a certain enchantress. And although this enchantress has lived, so to speak, in a civil marriage with a respectable man, she has an independent character and is an unapproachable fortress to everybody, just like a lawful wife—for she is virtuous, yes, holy Fathers, she is virtuous. Dmitri Fyodorovitch wants to open this fortress with a golden key, and that’s why he is insolent to me now and tries to get money out of me, though he has already wasted thousands on this enchantress. He’s forever borrowing money for the purpose. From whom, do you think? Shall I say, Mitya?”
“Be silent!” cried Dmitri. “Wait till I’ve gone. Don’t you dare slander the good name of an honorable girl in my presence! That you should say one word about her is an outrage, and I won’t allow it!”
